sections.title: Executive Summary
sections.content: As of March 2026, India operates 27,700 public electric vehicle (EV) charging stations with a charger-to-EV ratio of 1:235 [E1][E2]. The market is supported by government initiatives like the PM E-DRIVE scheme, which aims to add 72,300 public charging stations by March 2028 (verify the current status) [E3][E4]. Operating a charging station is a de-licensed activity, simplifying entry for new providers (verify the current status) [E5][E6].

sections.title: Market Insights
sections.content: Market estimates vary by source; for instance, Grand View Research reported the market generated $557.4 million in 2025, while Markets and Markets valued it at $129 million in 2026 [E7][E8]. These figures are not directly comparable as they originate from different sources that define the market differently. Demand is influenced by regional adoption, with Uttar Pradesh accounting for 20% of India's EV fleet and Karnataka representing 20% of the national charging network [E9][E10]. In Karnataka, two-wheelers make up 78% of the local EV market, highlighting the importance of segment-specific infrastructure [E11].

sections.title: Competitor Analysis
sections.content: The competitive landscape includes companies such as Tata Power and EZ Charge, both of which are actively building dense charging coverage across metro areas and highways [E12][E13]. While these firms are established, the market remains open due to the de-licensed nature of operating charging stations (verify the current status) [E5][E14].

sections.title: Opportunities and Risks
sections.content:
Opportunities:
• Financial support is available for charging projects through government programs like the PM E-DRIVE scheme and specialized green loans from banks such as SBI and Indian Bank (verify the current status) [E15][E16][E17][E18][E19].
• There is potential to integrate battery energy storage systems and second-life batteries into charging stations to improve efficiency and grid management [E20][E21].
• Small towns and rural areas present a specific opportunity for simple, rugged charging systems that prioritize ease of maintenance and local training [E22].
Risks:
• Most current EV chargers in India do not support vehicle-to-grid (V2G) technology, which allows cars to send power back to the electrical grid [E23].
• The previous FAME-II support scheme concluded in March 2024, and charging operators must navigate complex grid connection and billing requirements set by local Distribution Companies (DISCOMs) (verify the current status) [E24][E25].

sections.title: Recommendations
sections.content:
• Focus on developing charging infrastructure for two-wheelers, as they represent a significant portion of the market in key states like Karnataka [E11].
• Leverage available financial support, such as the PM E-DRIVE capital support or loans from institutions like SBI and Indian Bank, to manage initial setup costs (verify the current status) [E15][E18][E19][E26].
• Prioritize the installation of standardized charging connectors to ensure compatibility with national infrastructure requirements and streamline operations [E27][E28].

sections.title: Evidence Requiring Review
sections.content:
These 8 statements could not be fully confirmed, so they are not used in the findings above. The reason for each is shown in brackets. Please check them before using them.
• The Bureau of Indian Standards (BIS) is the national standards body of India responsible for formulating EV charging standards for the country [E29] (publication date unknown).
• IS-17017-Part-23 specifies requirements for DC charging stations with power output ranging from 50kW to 200kW [E30] (publication date unknown).
• IMARC estimated the India EV market size was $1.45 billion in 2025 [E31] (disagrees with another source).
• Expert Market Research stated the India EV market size reached $7.38 billion in 2025 [E32] (disagrees with another source).
• DC fast charging in India typically commands ₹12-18 per kWh [E33] (publication date unknown).
• AC charging in India ranges from ₹8-14 per kWh [E34] (publication date unknown).
• EV charging stations in India typically achieve gross margins of 30-50% after electricity costs [E35] (publication date unknown).
• EV charging stations in India achieve net margins of 15-25% after all operating expenses [E36] (publication date unknown).

sections.title: Glossary
sections.content:
Simple explanations of important terms used in this report. These definitions are explanatory notes, not research evidence.
- EV: An electric vehicle is a vehicle that uses one or more electric motors for propulsion.
- De-licensed: This refers to an activity that does not require a specific government license to operate.
- Battery energy storage systems: These are technologies that store electrical energy in batteries for later use to balance supply and demand.
- Second-life batteries: These are used electric vehicle batteries that are repurposed for stationary energy storage applications.
- Vehicle-to-grid: This is a system where electric vehicles can discharge stored energy back into the electrical power grid.
- DISCOMs: Distribution companies are entities responsible for the distribution of electricity to end users in a specific region.
- FAME-II: Faster Adoption and Manufacturing of Hybrid and Electric Vehicles is a government scheme designed to promote electric mobility.
- PM E-DRIVE: This is a government initiative aimed at expanding electric vehicle charging infrastructure and promoting electric mobility.
